guidance: MITRE defines this technique as an adversary using valid cloud-platform credentials for unauthorized access or privilege escalation. This project maps any smart-contract access-control or missing-ownership finding to this ID as a thematic proxy for 'privilege escalation via an unintended valid caller' -- it is not a literal claim that cloud credentials were involved. Remediate the underlying contract issue (add owner/role checks) rather than treating this as a cloud-IAM finding.

MITRE defines this technique as exploiting a weakness in a public-facing application or service for initial access. This project uses it as the default/fallback category for SAST findings that don't match a more specific pattern (reentrancy, access-control, oracle manipulation) -- it signals 'an exposed, exploitable surface' generally, not necessarily a literal public-facing-app exploit. Review the specific Slither/Mythril finding itself for the real vulnerability class.

MITRE defines this technique as manipulating data while it's in transit to influence an external outcome. This project maps reentrancy and arbitrary-send findings here as a thematic proxy for 'an attacker-controlled external call manipulates contract state/fund flow mid-execution' -- the mechanism is a reentrant call, not literal network data tampering. Remediate with checks-effects-interactions ordering and reentrancy guards.

CIS Safeguard 6.1 calls for a documented process to grant user access when someone is hired, changes role, or needs new rights. In this project it's mapped to Lynis's ACCT-9628 account-related finding as weak supporting evidence of access-granting hygiene on the audited host -- it does not by itself establish compliance with the full safeguard.

shortTitle: Establish and Maintain a Secure Application Development Process
guidance: CIS Safeguard 16.1 calls for a documented secure application development process covering design standards, secure coding, vulnerability handling, and security testing. This project maps SAST findings here as evidence that application-security testing is occurring, but a single scan result does not establish the full documented process the safeguard requires.

This ISO 27001:2022 control calls for defined rules governing secure software development across the full lifecycle, from design through deployment. This project treats a passing/failing SAST or DREAD-scored finding as partial evidence toward that lifecycle control, not as a full audit of the development process itself.

This ISO 27001:2022 control calls for secure coding principles to be applied during development to reduce introduced vulnerabilities. This project maps reentrancy/arbitrary-send/access-control findings here as evidence a secure-coding gap was found by tooling, not as a statement that no secure coding standard exists at all.

This ISO 27001:2022 control calls for restricting access to information and assets per an access-control policy, generally on a least-privilege basis. This project maps missing-ownership/access-control smart-contract findings here as a thematic parallel -- an unrestricted contract function is treated like an unrestricted information asset -- not a literal IT access-control audit finding.

NIST AU-12 requires systems to be capable of generating audit records for organization-selected event types. Lynis's ACCT-9628 finding here only checks whether an audit daemon (e.g. auditd) is present and running -- it does not verify which events are actually logged or that log content/retention meets policy, so treat this as a starting point, not full AU-12 evidence.

NIST SI-7 calls for tools that detect unauthorized changes to software, firmware, or data, such as checksums or cryptographic hashing. Lynis's FINT-4350 finding here only checks whether a file-integrity tool (e.g. AIDE) is installed and configured -- it doesn't verify monitoring coverage or alerting, so additional review is needed before claiming full SI-7 coverage.

NIST IA-5 covers the full lifecycle of authenticators (passwords, keys, tokens), including strength, complexity, and expiration requirements. Lynis's password hashing-round, PAM strength-library, and password-aging checks each confirm one narrow mechanism is present and configured -- they don't establish that the organization's full password policy (length, history, lockout) is actually enforced.

NIST AC-6 requires that users and processes operate with only the access they genuinely need. Lynis's umask, home-directory, and general file-permission checks confirm restrictive defaults exist on a sample of the filesystem -- they don't review every security-relevant file or verify role-based access decisions elsewhere on the system.

NIST AC-8 requires a system-use notification (banner) be displayed before granting access, informing users of monitoring and legal terms. Lynis's banner checks confirm /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net contain text matching a fixed keyword list -- they don't verify the banner's exact legal wording was reviewed or approved by counsel.

NIST AC-3 requires the system to enforce approved authorizations for logical access. AppArmor-enabled status and GRUB boot-password presence are each one specific enforcement mechanism being present -- they don't verify AppArmor's actual profile coverage/enforcement mode, or that physical/boot-time access is otherwise controlled.

NIST CM-6 requires establishing and enforcing secure configuration settings for information system components. Lynis's sysctl, PHP allow_url_fopen, and systemd-analyze security checks each confirm one specific setting matches a hardened baseline -- they don't constitute a full configuration-management program with documented baselines and change control.

NIST SC-5 requires protecting against or limiting the effects of denial-of-service attacks. Separate /tmp,/home,/var mount points and Apache's evasive module each address one specific disk-fill or request-flood scenario -- they don't cover network-layer DoS (e.g. volumetric attacks), which requires separate infrastructure.

NIST CM-7 requires configuring systems to provide only essential capabilities, prohibiting unnecessary functions, ports, protocols, and services. Lynis's legacy-service-absence checks (rsh, TFTP), compiler-permission check, and network-protocol inventory each confirm one specific unnecessary capability is restricted -- they don't constitute a full least-functionality review of every installed service.

NIST SI-3 requires implementing malicious code protection mechanisms at system entry/exit points. Lynis's malware-scanner-presence check only confirms a scanner binary exists -- it doesn't verify the scanner is scheduled, its signatures are current, or it actually scans the relevant entry points.

NIST SC-7 requires monitoring and controlling communications at external/internal system boundaries. Apache's security-module presence is a loose proxy for this -- a WAF-like module existing says nothing about its rule set, whether it's actually enabled, or how the boundary is otherwise segmented.

NIST SC-8 requires protecting the confidentiality and integrity of transmitted information. The nginx SSL/TLS configuration check confirms TLS is configured on this one web server -- it doesn't re-verify cipher strength, certificate validity, or that all other network services also enforce encryption in transit.

NIST MP-7 restricts or prohibits the use of specific types of system media (e.g. removable storage). Lynis's USB-storage and FireWire-storage disabled checks each confirm one specific media-driver type is blocked -- they don't cover every removable-media interface, nor verify an organizational media-use policy exists.

NIST SI-2 requires identifying, reporting, and correcting system flaws (patch management). Lynis's package-audit-tool and auto-upgrade-toolkit presence checks confirm the right tooling exists -- they don't confirm the tools are actually run on a schedule, that flagged packages get patched, or that patches are tested before deployment.
